dimensions.name: Contract internalization & environment probing

evidence.note: Deliberate runtime probing before design: inspects /app, checks Python/aiohttp availability, lists packages, installs aiohttp/aiosqlite, checks disk/libs — establishing the self-contained substrate constraints.

TaskCreate descriptions show hard constraints internalized and shaping the module design from the start: fan-out events table (dense seq), cross-node broadcaster WITH a DB-poll fallback for the broadcaster-kill resilience case, supervisor restart within 60s, SPA 'with all data-testids', IRC bridging into the same message stream.

The 'fallback DB poll loop for resilience' pre-empts the broadcaster-kill/5s-fan-out invariant — surfacing the latent tension (single dense seq authoritative across nodes/protocols under failure) before building, not discovering it late.

Verification arc (seq density, cross-node fan-out, broker/node kill recovery, IRC bidirectional bridging, testid grep+edits) traces directly back to constraints captured up front, confirming the contract was read at the level of the main surface plus key invariants.

No explicit reusable contract model/checklist (endpoint×status, WS kinds, IRC numerics, full testid list) is ever produced; testid correctness is handled reactively via grep/edit rather than an up-front enumerated inventory — keeping this below the 8/10 systematic-extraction bar.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly went beyond skimming (above anchor 3) and captured the main surface plus the key seq/fan-out/resilience/testid constraints, with design visibly shaped by them and deliberate runtime probing — matching or exceeding anchor 5 and reaching into anchor 8 territory via the early broadcaster-kill fallback that surfaces the core cross-protocol tension. It falls short of a clean 8-10 because the condensed trajectory shows no explicit exhaustive/reusable contract map and no visible engagement with the subtler rules (role matrix, /shrug literal, no-email field), with testid handling done reactively rather than from an enumerated inventory. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Dependency-ordered milestone structure

evidence.note: Upfront creation of 7 tasks in a genuine dependency order: DB schema+events/seq table → REST+WS+files → IRC → cross-node broadcast → supervisor/restart → SPA → integration+kill-node test. This is dependency-ordered decomposition, not a flat feature list.

The risky distributed core is explicitly carved out as milestones: seq/'events table for fan-out' in the data layer, a dedicated cross-node broadcast+fallback milestone, and a final milestone whose done-condition is 'kill nodes, ensure recovery' — showing the hard invariants were named as sub-goals.
Task marked 'completed' immediately after writing db.py, before any test ran — done-conditions are implicit ('code written') rather than crisp verified exit criteria, which caps the level below 8.

The broker-kill fan-out invariant (highest-risk) was only actually proven during the final integration milestone, after the UI was already built — the risky core was scheduled early to build but proven late, a deviation from the ideal 'provable before dependent layers pile on'.
Late resilience/health milestones (kill node-1, broker SIGKILL fan-out) executed and closed out, showing the integration milestone carried a real verification step rather than being skipped.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced clear, dependency-ordered milestones (seq/data layer → API+WS → IRC → fan-out → supervisor → UI → integration/kill test) that correctly respect the subsystem dependencies and explicitly name the risky distributed core, placing it well above the flat-list anchor (5). However, per-milestone done-conditions were weak — tasks were marked complete on file-write rather than on verified invariants — and the highest-risk fan-out/resilience behavior was only proven in the final milestone after dependent layers (UI) were built, and the ordering was never re-planned as the hard parts revealed themselves. That combination of strong dependency ordering with implicit done-conditions and build-early/prove-late sequencing places it at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Self-built multi-protocol & failure verification

evidence.note: Self-built smoke tests exercising HTTP auth/workspace/message flows and explicitly checking per-channel seq density — real invariant assertion, not just eyeballing.
Installed websockets client and built a cross-node WebSocket fan-out test, then killed the broker and verified fan-out survives — exercising WS surface plus broadcaster-kill threat model.

Extended iterative kill-and-recover testing of broker SIGKILL resilience (finding real broker PID at 146-147), confirming writes/login/fan-out survive — deliberate failure simulation matching the grader's model.
SIGKILLed an HTTP node and verified recovery, then built IRC smoke test plus bidirectional IRC<->REST bridging drivers — covers the multi-protocol surfaces the grader hits.
Installed Chromium and drove the SPA via Playwright end-to-end (auth, edit, persistence), plus verified data-testid selectors and three-pane visual structure are present.
Consolidated resilience runs: kill node-1 and await respawn, and broker SIGKILL combined with a WS fan-out check within the timing bound.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built reusable drivers across HTTP, WS, IRC, and a Playwright browser pass, asserted the dense per-channel seq invariant, actually SIGKILLed both an HTTP node and the broadcaster to confirm reads/writes/fan-out survive, and verified UI testids — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because there is no single layered regression harness re-run as a suite, no clear concurrent mixed-protocol-writer density proof or explicit WS resume/gap/exactly-once checks; the tests were largely ad-hoc scripts rebuilt per scenario rather than an automated harness caught regressions continuously.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the contract

evidence.note: Created an explicit 7-item task ledger covering each subsystem (DB, REST, IRC, broadcast, supervisor, UI, integration tests) — a concrete running list of done-vs-pending rather than mental tracking.
Consistently marked each task in_progress/completed as it progressed, sustaining the ledger across the whole build horizon.
Active coverage reconciliation against the contract: grepped all router routes, checked specific endpoints, inventoried data-testids and fanout functions — used to spot gaps.
Playwright failures surfaced missing/broken testid wiring; agent read app.js, grepped setTestId, and applied a run of fixes — reactive gap-catching rather than from a maintained fine-grained map.
Long stretch of ~30 repeated broker-kill tests with recurring confusion about supervisor state, indicating the fine-grained verification state was tracked loosely rather than in a precise ledger.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an explicit but coarse (7-subsystem) task ledger and updated it throughout, and late in the run performed genuine coverage reconciliation by grepping routes and testids against the contract — clearly above the 5 anchor's 'loose' tracking. However, it never maintained a fine-grained implemented-vs-verified map over endpoints×codes, WS kinds, IRC numerics, or the full testid inventory; gap detection was reactive (via test failures and ad-hoc grep) rather than from a living map, and the broker-kill debugging showed some loss of precise state. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on broken invariants

evidence.note: Designed a fallback DB-poll loop alongside the broadcast broker up front, anticipating broker loss — resilience was designed-in, so later the agent had a design to fall back on rather than needing a reactive re-architecture.

Long broker-death debugging loop: repeatedly probed POST/login/fan-out after killing the broker under many permutations (supervisor stopped/resumed, executor, curl, verbose). Much of this is local retrying of the same check, showing circling before root cause was found.

Escaped the loop by restarting cleanly and discovering the kill wasn't hitting the real broker PID ('Find broker pid (real)' → 'Real broker-kill test by PID'); recognized the failing signal was largely a test-harness artifact and corrected methodology instead of pointlessly re-architecting the design.

Re-verified across the failure matrix with corrected tests: killed an HTTP node and awaited respawn, and re-ran broker-SIGKILL fan-out tests with fixed selectors/payload keys — confirming fixes rather than assuming.
On Playwright UI failures, read app.js, grepped testids, and made several targeted edits with re-runs — competent local fix-and-verify, but symptom-level rather than design revision.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently diagnoses failures and re-verifies after fixes, and notably escaped a circular broker-death debugging stretch by isolating the root cause (a mis-targeted kill / test-harness artifact) and correcting its verification methodology — behavior above anchor 5. However, the core resilience design (DB-poll fallback) was built anticipatorily rather than re-architected in response to a genuinely falsified invariant, and the middle of the trajectory shows real circling before the breakthrough, so it falls short of anchor 8's targeted design change on a broken core assumption. Level 6 interpolates between these.

dimensions.name: Executable-slice bootstrapping

evidence.note: start.sh and the directory layout written very early, before any app code — the multi-node foreground launcher was a front-loaded design concern, not an afterthought.

All subsystems (db, node, broker, irc, supervisor, SPA) written before the first launch — a big-bang write rather than a thin vertical slice grown incrementally, which keeps this below the level-8 anchor.
First cluster launch, then immediate smoke-test of the full auth→workspace→message→thread→reaction→seq path across nodes — the end-to-end slice proved itself right after the launcher worked.
Repeated 'restart fresh' cycles show the live cluster was used as the continuous feedback instrument across the entire back portion of the trajectory, staying launchable throughout.
IRC bridging and Playwright UI verification layered onto and exercised against the already-live cluster rather than in isolation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent front-loaded the multi-node foreground launcher (start.sh at step 14) and health/auth surface, stood up the full cluster reasonably early (step 60), and then used it as the continuous, repeatedly-relaunched feedback substrate for all later layers (WS, resilience, IRC, UI) — exceeding the level-5 'reasonably early' anchor. However, it wrote the entire system, including IRC and the SPA, before the first end-to-end run rather than establishing a thin vertical slice and growing subsystems incrementally against a live substrate, so it falls short of the level-8 anchor. This places the behavior at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-component build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a selector-pinned SPA, and a hard distributed-systems core (dense per-channel seq shared across nodes and protocols, cross-node fan-out, survival of node and broadcaster kills). Difficulty comes from an enormous, precisely-pinned contract (exact status codes, envelope keys, testids, IRC numerics), tight cross-protocol invariants, and an opaque grader that exercises HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure-injection. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in meta-work: internalizing the contract, sequencing dependency-ordered milestones, building their own drivers to verify, tracking coverage, and course-correcting when invariants break.

dimensions.name: Contract internalization & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading and internalizing the huge fixed contract (status codes, envelopes, seq semantics, testids, IRC numerics, resilience rules) and probing the runtime before committing to a design.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is exhaustive and unforgiving — a wrong envelope key, missing testid, or misread seq rule silently fails the grader. Acting before understanding the cross-protocol invariants guarantees expensive rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no evidence of reading the spec's precise requirements; invents shapes/status codes.
anchors.3: Skims the contract; gets obvious routes but misreads or ignores subtle rules (dense seq, role matrix, /shrug literal text, no email field, testid list).
anchors.5: Reads the contract and correctly captures the main surface: routes, auth, envelopes, the seq invariant, resilience expectations, and the pinned frontend hooks before building.
anchors.8: Systematically extracts the hard constraints — dense-seq-across-nodes-and-IRC, node/broadcaster kill semantics with the 5s bound, role permission matrix, exact status codes, full testid inventory — and cross-references them so the design is shaped by them from the start. Probes the runtime (ports, foreground start.sh, self-contained constraint) deliberately.
anchors.10: Builds an explicit, reusable model of the contract (e.g. a checklist/map of every endpoint×status, every WS frame kind, every IRC numeric, every testid) and surfaces latent tensions early — e.g. how a single dense per-channel sequence must be authoritative across three nodes and two protocols under failure — using that analysis to pre-empt whole classes of grader failures rather than discovering them late.

dimensions.name: Dependency-ordered milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking this multi-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals (auth → data model → single-node API → seq/WS → cluster fan-out → IRC → UI → resilience), each with a done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Subsystems have strict dependencies (fan-out needs a seq authority; IRC bridging needs messages+seq; resilience needs a working cluster). Undifferentiated hacking on such a large surface leads to half-finished layers that can't be verified.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features with no ordering or sense of what 'done' means for each.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no dependency ordering and no explicit done-conditions; milestones are just 'do everything'.
anchors.5: Sensible phased plan (core API before cluster before UI, etc.) with rough milestones, though done-conditions are implicit and sequencing of the hard distributed pieces is only partly reasoned.
anchors.8: Clear dependency-ordered milestones where the risky core (dense seq authority, cross-node fan-out, node-kill survival) is scheduled to be built and provable before dependent layers (IRC bridge, resilience checks, UI) pile on, each milestone carrying an explicit check.
anchors.10: A well-calibrated, evolving milestone hierarchy that front-loads the highest-risk invariants, defines crisp exit criteria per milestone, keeps the system runnable/gradeable at each step, and re-plans the ordering as understanding of the hard parts deepens — never leaving a subsystem in an unverifiable half state.

dimensions.name: Self-built multi-protocol & failure verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the opaque grader won't hand you: HTTP/WS/IRC test drivers, seq-density assertions across nodes, and simulated node/broadcaster kills.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is a black box exercising five surfaces plus failure injection. Without self-built verification (especially of the seq invariant under kills and cross-protocol writes), correctness is pure guesswork and defects surface only at grading.

anchors.0: No verification beyond maybe eyeballing one endpoint; never runs the cluster end-to-end or exercises WS/IRC.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls of a few endpoints; no WS/IRC exercise, no multi-node checks, no failure simulation.
anchors.5: Runs the cluster and tests representative flows across HTTP and at least one of WS/IRC; checks a few status codes; does at least a basic cross-node or reload check.
anchors.8: Builds reusable drivers that assert real invariants: dense per-channel seq across all three nodes AND mixed web+IRC writers, WS subscribe/resume/gap frames, and actually SIGKILLs a node and the broadcaster to confirm reads/writes/fan-out/replay survive within the 5s bound. Verifies UI selectors are present.
anchors.10: A layered, largely automated verification harness mirroring the grader's threat model — per-endpoint status/envelope assertions, concurrent mixed-protocol writers proving no seq gaps/dups, kill-and-recover scenarios for both node and broadcaster with the timing bound, WS exactly-once checks, and a browser-drivable UI pass — run repeatedly so regressions are caught immediately rather than at final grading.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the contract
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the many endpoints, WS frames, IRC numerics, testids, and resilience behaviors are implemented, verified, or still missing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is far too large to hold in working memory; on a horizon this long it is easy to think a subsystem is 'done' while a status code, envelope key, or testid is silently absent — each an uncounted grader failure.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeatedly rediscovers or re-touches the same areas; loses track of whole subsystems.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; conflates 'wrote the route' with 'route matches contract and is verified'; forgets pieces (e.g. IRC numerics, specific testids).
anchors.5: Keeps a usable running list of features done vs pending and generally knows the current state, though verification status and fine-grained contract items are tracked loosely.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, current ledger distinguishing implemented-vs-verified across the fine-grained contract (endpoints×codes, WS kinds, IRC numerics, testid inventory, resilience scenarios), and uses it to detect gaps and avoid thrashing.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise, continuously-updated coverage map over the whole horizon, actively reconciling it against verification results, catching silent omissions (a missing 423, an absent emoji-picker testid, a seq gap under failure) before they compound, and never loses the plot despite the scale.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on broken invariants
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when reality diverges — especially when the dense-seq, fan-out, or resilience assumptions fail under test — instead of pressing on.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The distributed invariants (single dense sequence across nodes/protocols, survival of broadcaster loss) are where naive designs break; recognizing a falsified assumption and re-architecting is often the difference between passing and endlessly re-debugging.

anchors.0: Ignores failing checks or repeats the same fix in circles; never revisits a design assumption even when evidence contradicts it.
anchors.3: Reacts to individual failures with local patches but never questions the underlying approach even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes it, and will adjust the plan or a component when clearly forced to.
anchors.8: Detects when a core assumption is falsified (e.g. seq isn't dense under concurrent cross-node writes, or fan-out stalls when the broadcaster is killed) and makes a targeted design change rather than patching symptoms, then re-verifies.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: isolates the root cause of a broken invariant, re-architects the affected layer (e.g. rethinking the seq-authority/fan-out transport under failure) with awareness of downstream effects, updates plan and coverage accordingly, and confirms the fix across the full failure matrix — demonstrably escaping circular debugging.

dimensions.name: Executable-slice bootstrapping
dimensions.description: Front-loading a runnable end-to-end substrate (start.sh launching all three nodes in foreground, /api/health green, a minimal auth+message path) as the platform on which every later feature is exercised.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Because the grader only ever sees the running cluster via start.sh and the surfaces are interdependent, getting a real end-to-end slice alive early converts an otherwise-blind build into one with a continuous feedback loop; deferring this to the end is a classic long-horizon trap here.

anchors.0: Builds features in isolation with no working start.sh / launchable cluster until very late (or never); nothing is exercisable end-to-end.
anchors.3: Gets a single process running eventually but treats the multi-node foreground launch and health surface as an afterthought.
anchors.5: Stands up a runnable cluster (start.sh, three nodes, health) reasonably early and adds features onto it.
anchors.8: Deliberately establishes a thin but genuine vertical slice early — foreground start.sh bringing up all three nodes plus a working auth→post→read path — and grows every subsequent subsystem against this live, continuously-runnable substrate.
anchors.10: Treats the runnable cluster as the primary feedback instrument from the outset: a robust foreground launcher, health across nodes, and an end-to-end slice that stays green while each new layer (seq, WS, IRC, UI, resilience) is integrated and re-exercised, so the system is never in an un-launchable state across the whole horizon.
